title: Blitz chess: five minutes for everything
description: In blitz chess each player gets only a few minutes for the whole game. The clock stops being furniture and becomes a second opponent — and that changes which moves are good.

body.heading: A second opponent
paragraphs: In a slow game you can spend twenty minutes on one hard move. In blitz, with five minutes for everything, that same move costs you the game even if it is brilliant — the flag falls, the clock reads zero, and the position no longer matters.

So blitz rewards a different skill: deciding quickly which moves are good enough. Strong blitz players do not calculate less deeply on every move; they save their seconds for the two or three moments that truly decide the game.

body.heading: What blitz teaches
paragraphs: Blitz exposes what you actually know. Openings you merely memorised collapse under time pressure, while patterns you truly understand appear instantly. That is why coaches use short blitz sessions as a diagnostic, not just as fun.

Play it as training, not as a verdict. A blunder at one minute left is information about your patterns, not your worth as a player — write it down, check it slowly later, and let the slow game teach what the fast one revealed.

takeaway: Blitz makes the clock a second opponent: spend your seconds only on the moves that decide the game, and treat fast blunders as lessons for slow chess.
